surfaces.part: large boulder pile, light upper facets
left rock cluster, light top facets

answer.evidence: The column at x=25 shows light top facets (L=196) in rows 9-19, then a mid-tone edge line at row 20 (L=152). Darker shadow follows in rows 21-22 (L=98), and the darker front faces run through rows 23-29. The left cluster at x=13 has the same pattern: light rows 12-15, an edge at row 16, then darker faces. The silhouette widens from 8 px at row 7 to 45 px at row 23 and tapers to 2 px at row 31, giving a lumpy heap with lit upper planes and shaded south faces. It is a scatter of debris, so there is no single clean slab top, but the heap does show top planes above front faces.

styleAnswer.evidence: The rock pile has about 5 grey steps (pale highlight, light, mid, dark, outline) and each stone is shaded separately, with no flat 5x5 areas (0% near-flat). It carries 10 visible tones per tile, about level with the hedge (9) but below the stall (17) and well (20). The weak point is the outline: 100% of its dark edge pixels are near-neutral, and the picture shows a fairly uniform dark grey-black line around every stone. That is the 'sticker' look. The well's stones, by contrast, have tinted dark edges (33% neutral), and the hedge and stall have almost none (0% and 1%). Texture on the stone faces is modest, with few grain dots or cracks. When in doubt, fail, so it fails on the neutral outline and slightly shallow texture.

answer.evidence: A scattered pile of irregular rocks, shown as a lumpy faceted silhouette (width grows from 8 at row 7 to 45 at row 23, then tapers to 2 at row 31). The shading is faceted light and dark patches on each stone, with no band ending in a front-edge line, no eave shadow, no ellipse and no roof plane. The dark base at rows 28-30 is a ground shadow. It is debris lying on the floor, not a box-like body with a distinct top and front face. The structure is neither a clear three-quarter volume nor a clear front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The rock pile reads as a grey cluster with about 4 lightness steps (light highlight, two mid greys, dark crevice) and a few per-stone highlights. Visible tones per tile are 10, close to the hedge (9) but well below the well (20) and stall (17). Near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no flat fills. The dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, so the silhouette is a uniform colourless dark outline with no tint. Stone is a neutral material, but the outline still reads as the 'sticker' look, not a selective dark tone of the adjacent stone. Beodeul's hedge and well use tinted edges (0% and 33% neutral). The stones are shaded in only a few steps, with less per-stone texture than the references' 5-6 step ramps. With the outline and the lower density, I would not accept it beside the references without more work.

answer.evidence: This is an irregular rubble heap. In the column scans the upper rows are light facets (x=25 rows 9-19 at L=196/152; x=13 rows 12-16; x=36 rows 14-17). Below them the rows are darker, shaded south-facing faces (x=25 rows 21-24 at L=98-125; x=13 rows 17-21; x=36 rows 19-23). The silhouette widens from 8 px at row 7 to 45 px at row 23, then tapers to a dark base at rows 27-31. That gives a lit upper surface over a shaded front face of about 10 rows, so it reads as a 3/4-view heap rather than a flat slab or a front elevation. No isometric side face is drawn.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a grey rock pile with about 4 lightness steps (highlight, light, mid, dark). Each rock is outlined in a dark grey that is fully neutral: 100% of its dark edge pixels are near-neutral, with no tint of the neighbouring material. The references (hedge 0%, stall 1%, well 33%) use tinted outlines and separate some forms by value alone. The candidate's uniform dark edge around every rock gives the 'sticker' look. Its 10 visible tones per tile roughly match the hedge (9) but sit well below the well (20) and stall (17). There is no flat fill (0% near-flat), and the rocks have some facets and speckle. They are not shaded stone by stone with the 5-6 steps Beodeul uses. A careful artist would likely call it flatter than the references, and when in doubt the rule is to fail.

answer.evidence: A pile of faceted rocks with an irregular silhouette (width grows from 8 at row 7 to 45 at row 23, then narrows to 2 at row 31). The pile is shaded in light and dark facets, with the lightest facets (L=196) at the top of the boulders and darker facets lower down. There is no front-edge line followed by eave shadow, no ellipse and no roof plane, so no distinct horizontal top surface is drawn. This is scattered rubble, so a rounded heap shape is natural. Nothing reads as a rim or a flat slab. The dark bottom rows 28-30 look like a ground shadow, not a front face. The pile reads as an irregular heap with facets rather than a clear top and front structure.

styleAnswer.evidence: The rock pile has about 4 grey lightness steps (highlight, light, mid, dark) and a few per-stone facets, but the stones are not shaded one by one with the depth the references show. The measured outline is 100% near-neutral, with no tint, against 0-1% for the hedge and cheese stall and 33% for the well. The pile therefore reads as a uniform dark grey/black line around the whole silhouette, which is the sticker look, not an adjacent-material dark tone. Visible tones per tile (10) match the hedge (9) but are well below the stall (17) and well (20), and there are no flat fills (0% near-flat). It is acceptable in density but shallower in shading and outline craft than the Beodeul standard, so it fails.
